name: Shrimp hop
rodTip: Tip down, in the water, pointed straight along the line. Every inch of slack between rod tip and fly is an inch the fly does not move and a hook you will not set.
imitates: A shrimp flushed out of the bottom: two or three panicked backward hops, then it freezes and tries to disappear.
cue: The line comes tight, or you feel weight, DURING THE STOP — almost never during the strip. Strip until it stops moving, then wait with the line pinched.
mistake: Continuous stripping. A shrimp that never stops is a shrimp no bonefish has ever seen, and the eat has nowhere to happen.
notes: The default flats retrieve. Short and sharp, then genuinely still — count it out if you have to.

name: Crab drop
rodTip: Tip down and still. Your job after the cast is mostly to do nothing convincingly.
imitates: A crab that has been seen, drops flat to the bottom, and stops. It does not swim away — swimming away is the one thing a crab cannot do.
cue: Watch the fish, not the fly. The tip-down — nose to the bottom, tail up — IS the eat. Come tight then, with the line hand, and keep pulling.
mistake: Stripping once the fish has committed. A crab that swims off is a crab that was never real, and it is the single most common way a permit shot is lost.
notes: One small twitch to get attention if it has not seen the fly. After that, dead.

name: Crab crawl
rodTip: Tip down and close to the water.
imitates: A crab picking its way along the bottom, or a soft-shell that cannot get anywhere fast.
cue: Often a visible turn and a pounce in shallow water. In dirty water, weight on the line.
mistake: Moving it too far. Two inches at a time is a crawl; six inches at a time is a fleeing baitfish.
notes: The redfish and molting-crab answer, and the fallback when a drop has not been noticed.

name: Fleeing baitfish
rodTip: Tip in the water, rod tucked under your arm if you want two-handed speed.
imitates: A single minnow that has broken from the school and is running for its life. Nothing about it hesitates.
cue: The eat is a freight train mid-strip. Do not stop stripping when you feel it — keep pulling until the fish is on.
mistake: Pausing. This is the one retrieve where the pause kills you: a fly that stops is a fly a fast predator has time to inspect and refuse.
notes: Long smooth pulls, not short jabs. Two-handed stripping is worth learning for this.

name: Wounded baitfish
imitates: A minnow that cannot keep up — it darts, then falls out of the school and hangs.
cue: Line goes tight on the hang. Fish take a struggling baitfish at their leisure, and that leisure happens in the pause.
mistake: Treating it like the fleeing retrieve. The whole point is the hesitation; if you never let it hang you are fishing a different fly.
notes: The change-up when fish are chasing and refusing a straight fast strip.

name: Slow swim
rodTip: Tip low and pointed at the fly through the whole retrieve.
imitates: Something swimming steadily across and away from the fish — never at it. The angle is most of the presentation.
cue: You see the mouth open and white. Keep stripping through it, then strip-strike hard, more than once.
mistake: Lifting the rod. A trout set on a tarpon pulls the fly out of a bony mouth and ends the shot.
notes: Lead the fish, let the fly sink to their level, then swim it away. A fly moving toward a tarpon turns it off.

name: Pop and hang
rodTip: Tip down and to the side so the strip makes noise rather than lifting the fly.
imitates: Something struggling on the surface, making a commotion and then going still.
cue: The take is visual and violent. Wait until you feel weight before setting — setting on the splash pulls it away.
mistake: Setting on sight. The pause is also where you lose fish by striking at the boil instead of the pull.
notes: The pause is the fly. Two pops, four seconds of nothing, repeat.

name: Worm swim
imitates: A worm swimming feebly in a current it cannot fight.
cue: A soft, almost casual take in the drift.
mistake: Stripping it like a baitfish. In a worm hatch the fly should be barely under its own power.
notes: Let the current do most of the work; the strips are just to keep contact.

name: Dead drift
rodTip: Lead the fly with the tip, keeping contact without pulling. On a tight line, the sighter should bend, not straighten.
imitates: Something with no say in the matter, going wherever the current takes it. Which is most of what trout eat.
cue: A hesitation, a tick, a sighter that stops or jumps upstream. If you are waiting to feel it, you are already late.
mistake: Drag. Any pull across the current is a signal to the fish that this one is not food.
notes: Set downstream and low, not straight up.

name: Drift then lift
rodTip: Dead drift, then raise the tip steadily at the end of the swing and let the flies climb.
imitates: A pupa leaving the bottom for the surface — which is the moment in a caddis emergence that fish actually key on.
cue: The take on the lift is unmistakable and often violent. Keep the rod steady and let the fish hook itself.
mistake: Picking up to recast the instant the drift ends, which skips the best three seconds of it.
notes: The lift is the imitation, not the fly.

name: Drift and twitch
rodTip: Tip up enough to hold line off the water, twitch with the line hand not the rod.
imitates: An adult caddis skittering, or a terrestrial kicking after it lands.
cue: A splashy take, usually within a second of the twitch.
mistake: Twitching so hard the fly drags. One inch is a twitch; six inches is a mistake.
notes: Drift it drag-free first. The twitch is what you try when the drag-free drift is refused.

name: Streamer strip
rodTip: Tip down and in the water, rod pointed at the fly so the strip actually moves it.
imitates: A sculpin or small fish bolting for cover and stopping short, exposed.
cue: The eat comes on the fall, as the fly turns and drops. A loop knot doubles how much it turns.
mistake: Stripping the fly all the way to the bank without a pause — and then lifting to recast just as a following fish makes up its mind.
notes: Vary the pause before you vary the fly. Same streamer, longer hang, is usually the fix.
